rv.q: I went in fearing the worst, in all honesty, but this is a production that, even if it is never going to supplant the film, at least delivers moments of communal intensity.
None of it is half as shocking, entertaining or as poignant as the film.
It's a depressing concoction, with misjudged songs and a plot as obscure as an addict's mumblings.
But it's a very awkward beast: rambling, blunt, shallow and weirdly anodyne.
Sadly, this stage musical – scripted by Welsh, who also co-wrote the music and lyrics with Stephen McGuinness – is a misguided muddle.
The attempt fails dismally, despite the admirable efforts of the leading man Lewis Kidd.
This misfiring adaptation is the perfect case in point that not every story should be turned into a musical.
I can't tell you what this show wants to be but it definitely doesn't want to be a musical.
Ultimately it's the ineptitude rather than the tricky subject matter that sinks Trainspotting The Musical.
Trainspotting feels like an unsatisfying cash grab that leaves everyone feeling robbed.
I'll be blunt when I say this is without a doubt the worst show in the West End this year, and a contender for the biggest train wreck ever seen on a West End stage.

cn.t: Critics savage this ill-conceived adaptation as leaden and misconceived, with Welsh's gritty novel proving utterly incompatible with musical theatre. Despite a strong cast, the show fails to capture the film's edgy energy.
